pairs.title: Printing and formatting

notes.html: print puts a space between its arguments in both, and sep=", " (or any other text) replaces it.

A bare float prints differently. Python's print(x) writes the shortest digits that read back as the same double; Viv's print(x) writes six significant digits, as C's %g does. Each language has the other's form: fmt(x) in Viv, f"{x:g}" in Python.

f-strings are the same on both sides for these specs: {x}, {x=}, {x:.3f}, {x:10.4f}, {word!r}. The counts in this program are numbers, not Ints, so an integer is written with :d ({count:d}); without it, f"{count}" would be 3.0.
for i in range(count) is for i to count. A loop body is in braces instead of indented.
Python's assert statements become assertions inside a Viv test block, which prints one PASS formats line.

pairs.reason: Two lines print differently and are left out of the comparison. Python's round(2.5) is 2, because Python rounds a tie to the even neighbor; Viv's round(2.5) is 3, because Viv rounds a tie away from zero. Python prints a boolean as True or False, and Viv prints it as true or false.
pairs.reasonHtml: Two lines print differently and are left out of the comparison. Python's round(2.5) is 2, because Python rounds a tie to the even neighbor; Viv's round(2.5) is 3, because Viv rounds a tie away from zero. Python prints a boolean as True or False, and Viv prints it as true or false.

notes.html: A Viv number is a 64-bit float unless the program declares an Int; this program uses numbers only. a // b and a % b on numbers follow Python's rules for floats (the remainder takes the sign of b), so -17 // 5 is -4 and -17 % 5 is 3 on both sides.
Power is ^ in Viv and ** in Python. Both are right-associative, so 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 is 512.
sqrt, exp, floor and the rest are builtins in Viv; Python imports them from math. Viv has no pi: the program names the constant.
elif is else if, and the Viv code here puts else on its own line after the closing brace.
The conditional expression "even" if a % 2 == 0 else "odd" is the same in both; only the branch chosen is computed.
Python chains comparisons (0 < a < 20); Viv writes 0 < a and a < 20.

Python keeps ints and floats apart when it prints: 17 // 5 is the int 3 and 17 / 5 is the float 3.4. Viv's print writes any number with six significant digits and drops a trailing .0, so the whole numbers match Python's ints, and the Viv side wraps the fractions in fmt(...) to get Python's full digits.

pairs.name: loops
pairs.title: Loops

notes.html: for i in range(n) is for i to n; range(a, b, s) is for i from a to b by s, and a negative step counts down in both. reversed(range(n)) is for i to n reversed.
Viv's print always ends the line; there is no end=" ". The Viv side builds the line in a string and prints it once.

viv lint refuses an integer literal other than 0, 1 and 2 as a loop bound, so the Viv side names its bounds (FIRST, LAST, STEP). Python has no such rule; the Python side names the ones that mean something.

enumerate, zip, the comprehension [p * p for p in primes] and the if-expression n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1 are the same in both. (primes * primes would also multiply element by element in Viv.)
A comprehension's for takes Viv's loop heads: for c from 1 to TABLE where Python writes for c in range(1, TABLE).
continue and break are the same. found.append(k) is found = append(found, k): an append gives back a new array, written by rebinding the name.
A comparison of two arrays is elementwise in Viv, so a test of equality is all(found == [3, 5]).

notes.html: Viv has no default arguments and no keyword arguments. The Viv side writes the general function with every parameter (greet_with) and a short one that fills in the default (greet).
A docstring works the same way: a bare string as the first statement of a def documents it and does nothing when it runs.
return lo, hi, mean and lo, hi, mean = f(xs) are the same in both. In Viv the unpacking must be a statement of its own: print(f(xs)) is refused.
A lambda is fn(x) -> expr instead of lambda x: expr. A def name and a lambda are both values that can be passed and called.
min, max and sum take an array in Viv as they take a list in Python.
Python's print(lo, hi, mean) writes each float in full; the Viv side uses fmt(...) to get the same digits (see Printing and formatting).

# @@ imports
PI = 3.141592653589793

# @@ composite Simpson's rule
def simpson_rule(f, a, b, n) {
    if n % 2 == 1 {
        n += 1
    }
    h = (b - a) / n
    s = f(a) + f(b)
    for i from 1 to n {
        s += (4 if i % 2 == 1 else 2) * f(a + i * h)
    }
    return s * h / 3
}

# @@ the error falls as h^4
exact = 1.0 - cos(1.0)
prev = 0.0
for n in [4, 8, 16, 32] {
    err = abs(simpson_rule(fn(x) -> sin(x), 0.0, 1.0, n) - exact)
    ratio = f"{prev / err:6.2f}" if prev > 0 else "     -"
    print(f"n = {n:2d}  error = {err:.3e}  ratio = {ratio}")
    prev = err
}

print(f"integral of exp(-x^2) = {g:.12f}, sqrt(pi) = {sqrt(PI):.12f}")

test "Gaussian" {
    assert_near(g, sqrt(PI), 1e-10)
    assert_near(simpson(fn(x) -> exp(-x * x), -6.0, 6.0, POINTS), g, 1e-12)

notes.html: np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]) is the literal [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]. np.eye(2) * 2.0 has no builtin twin; the Viv side writes the matrix out.
A @ B is the matrix product and A * B the elementwise product in both.
A.T is transpose(A); A.shape is shape(A), which unpacks into rows, cols; A.size is numel(A).
A.sum() is sum(A). There is no axis= argument, so row and column sums are loops.
A > 1.5 gives an array of 1.0 and 0.0 in Viv (booleans in NumPy); both multiply the same way.
sqrt applies to every element of an array, as np.sqrt does. Viv's round takes no digit count, so rounding to 6 decimals is round(C * 1e6) / 1e6.
tolist() on the Python side and fmt(...) on the Viv side print a matrix the same way, [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]].

notes.html: Viv's own srand(seed) and rand() are a Park-Miller generator, not NumPy's. To draw the same numbers as np.random.default_rng(42), the Viv side uses lib/nprandom, a Viv port of NumPy's PCG64 generator and its methods, brought in with #! use lib/nprandom/generator.

The generator is an array of state that each call updates: rng.random() is npr_pcg_double(rng), rng.integers(1, 7) is 1 + npr_gn_bounded(rng, 5) (the bound is inclusive), rng.shuffle(deck) is npr_gn_shuffle(rng, deck) and rng.standard_normal() is npr_gn_normal(rng).
The library draws one number per call, so the vector calls rng.random(N) become loops. The draws must come in NumPy's order: all of x, then all of y, not the two interleaved.
np.count_nonzero(x * x + y * y < 1.0) is sum(...) of the comparison, which is an array of 1.0 and 0.0.

npr_gn_normal gives NaN where NumPy's value depends on the platform's log1p (about one draw in 4000 falls in that tail). The test checks that none of these 1000 draws did: all(z == z) is false if any is NaN.
z.std() divides by M, as the Viv formula does.

notes.html: The Python gradient is derived by hand: for the mean squared error, 2 X^T (X w - y) / n. The Viv gradient is grad(loss, w, X, y): the compiler writes the reverse pass of loss itself, and every engine runs that generated code. Nothing on the Viv side states the formula.

Both check the gradient against central differences with H = 1e-6; the Python side does it in one comprehension over np.eye(2), the Viv side in a loop that builds each unit vector (Viv has no eye yet).
grad(f, w, ...) differentiates with respect to the first argument and passes the rest through unchanged, and the result has the shape of w.
For one variable, Python writes the derivative df out (product rule). Viv's deriv(fn(x) -> sin(x) * x * x, 1.3) computes it in forward mode.
w0.copy() is copy(w0); X.T @ r would be transpose(X) @ r, but the Viv side never needs it.
The descent prints the same loss to 8 decimals in both, although the gradients are computed by different formulas: they agree to rounding.

notes.html: The Viv column is the program lib/gpt/story_gpt.viv runs, with its #! use lines expanded by hand: lib/gpt/gpt.viv and the defs it calls from lib/nn, lib/polar, lib/optim and lib/random, written in the same style as lib/gpt (one-line steps, comprehensions for arrays of records and for the batch). Defs are moved so that each layer sits in the same region as in the Python classes. Three edits: every step's loss is printed to six decimals; the optimizers' settings, records in lib/optim, are constants here; and Newton-Schulz reads Muon's coefficients and step count from those constants, as the Python's reads them from its defaults, where lib/polar's takes them as arguments. The NumPy program writes its layers and its optimizer out, so this program does too; the PyTorch pair (tiny_gpt_torch) imports them from lib/nn, lib/optim and lib/random, as the PyTorch program imports torch.

The Python column is what a NumPy programmer would write from scratch: a Config dataclass, one class per layer (Embedding, Head, Attention, MLP, Block, GPT), each holding its weights in a dict and caching what its backward needs on self, and an optimizer that walks named_parameters(). The Viv model is the same tree as records: Gpt { tok, pos, blocks: [Block], unembed }, Block { attn, mlp }, Attention { heads: [Head], Wo }, Head { Wq, Wk, Wv }, Mlp { up, down }, and a matrix is read where it is (b.mlp.up, h.Wq). The Python backward pass is written by hand; the Viv program's is value_and_grad(sequence_loss, model, ...), which the compiler writes from the forward pass and which gives a Gpt of gradients. The Viv optimizer updates the model in place, for_leaves(muon_update, model.blocks, g.blocks, m.blocks, lr_scale) for the blocks' matrices and adam_update for the other three, where the Python walks named_parameters(). Both train the same model (6,560 parameters, 2 blocks, 2 heads, width 16) for 30 steps with Muon on the matrices inside the blocks and Adam on the embeddings and the output map, then sample 24 characters.

The two programs print the same text. Printed with 17 digits, the 30 losses differ by at most 8.9 × 10−16, and the sampled text is the same string. The weights are the same because the Python side replays Viv's generator (Minstd: Park-Miller MINSTD, Box-Muller for the normals, the inverted cumulative sum for the sample), not np.random.default_rng: lib/gpt draws with srand and rand, not with lib/nprandom. Both sum a row along its last axis in NumPy's pairwise order (Viv's sum, mean and amax along an axis follow NumPy's). The rest of the difference is the order of the sums in @ (NumPy calls BLAS, which blocks its sums its own way), the order of the hand-written backward pass against the generated one, and the last bit of exp, log and cos, which Viv computes with its own libm.

A third program, tiny_gpt.phrased.viv (the "Viv in phrases" column), is the Viv column with the phrases lib/gpt, lib/nn and lib/random declare and use: take the causal mask of size T, take the softmax of each row of S, take the cross-entropy of gpt_forward(m, x) against y, take the last len(m.pos) elements of out. Each phrase is the call it stands for, so it prints the same bytes. The phrases that looked a matrix up in a flat parameter vector (take the query matrix of this head) are gone with the vector: the code reads the matrix where it is.

Both programs batch the four sequences of a step into one (4, 8, 16) array and let @ and the reductions work along the last axes: @ on a stack of matrices multiplies each matrix of the stack, as NumPy's does, so train calls value_and_grad once per step, on the whole batch.

notes.html: The Python column is the model of tiny_gpt in PyTorch: nn.Module subclasses, nn.Linear and nn.Embedding layers, F.scaled_dot_product_attention(..., is_causal=True), F.cross_entropy, torch.optim.Adam with a LambdaLR schedule, and Muon as an 11-line torch.optim.Optimizer subclass. There is no backward code: loss.backward() fills every p.grad, which is why its loss and backward regions hold only a comment. It is the reference for what the Viv program would look like with autograd, arrays of modules and batched tensors. It needs torch (run with 2.2.2, in float64 on one thread).

The Viv column imports what the torch program imports: #! use lib/nn for attention (one causal head, as F.scaled_dot_product_attention(..., is_causal=True)), softmax_rows, rmsnorm, relu2, cross_entropy and embedding (the row lookup of nn.Embedding); #! use lib/optim for adam_update and muon_update, which update one matrix and its memories in place with the settings in an AdamSettings or MuonSettings record; and #! use lib/random for randn_matrix and choice. It is the program lib/gpt/story_gpt.viv runs with lib/gpt/gpt.viv copied in, and prints the same bytes as the written-out Viv of the NumPy pair (tiny_gpt): all 30 losses and every trained weight to 17 digits, and the sample, in the interpreter, in C and in wasm. Its model is the same tree as the torch modules, as records: Gpt { tok, pos, blocks: [Block], unembed }, Block { attn, mlp }, Attention { heads: [Head], Wo }, Head { Wq, Wk, Wv }; its gradient is value_and_grad(sequence_loss, model, ...), a Gpt; and optimizer_step is for_leaves(muon_update, model.blocks, g.blocks, m.blocks, lr_scale, MUON_OPT) and three adam_update calls, where torch calls o.step() on each optimizer.

The outputs are the same text. Printed with 17 digits, the 30 losses differ from Viv's by at most 6.7e-16. The weights are copied from the same MINSTD draws (init_from fills each layer in the order lib/gpt lays them out, transposed where nn.Linear stores (out, in)), and the samples use the same draws. Muon's Newton-Schulz step returns the matrix unchanged when its norm is zero, as lib/polar does: at the first step the output map is zero, so every block matrix has a zero gradient, and dividing by the norm would give NaN.

torch 2.2 has no F.rms_norm and no Muon; both are written out here, in 2 and 11 lines (plus the 9 of newton_schulz). Viv imports both from its libraries, so the optimizer region is shorter in Viv (8 lines against 20). The torch program writes Minstd (12 lines) only to draw the weights and the samples Viv draws; Viv's random draws come from lib/random.

Lines are code lines: blank lines, comments and docstrings are not counted; characters are those lines' characters. A lookup is a read of a size from the configuration record (cfg.<field>, c.<field>); torch's self.q(x) is not counted, and neither is Viv's h.Wq. study/compare/measure.py counts them.

The Python side writes the runner itself, in a few lines, so the two print the same verdicts. pytest or unittest would find the test_ functions and print their own report instead.
A test name in Viv is a string with spaces; in Python it is a function name.
assert cond is assert_true(cond), and math.isclose(a, b, abs_tol=t) is assert_near(a, b, t). assert_near, assert_lt, assert_gt and assert_allclose print the numbers they compared when they fail.
all(x > 0 for x in w) works in Viv too; all(w > 0) is the array form: the comparison makes an array of 1.0 and 0.0 and all reads it.
normalize is one array expression in Viv, xs / sum(xs), where the Python list needs a comprehension.
A top-level assert_true outside any test prints its own line; the pairs on this site put their checks in test blocks.
